name: sm-02-utility-and-limits
title: Utility & limits — what a cheap emulator buys, and where emulation ends
claim:
The honest by-product of sm-01 — a cheap LINEAR emulator of coarse growth —
is genuinely useful: it pays back its 8 training simulations after ~8
evaluations and sweeps 5,000 trajectories in 0.02 s (vs ~24 h on the WCM,
~3.8e6× per trajectory). Its limits are explicit: it emulates a smooth,
low-dimensional observable view, not the cell's high-dimensional hidden state.
question:
Given that the linear emulator (not the neural net) is the model that works
for coarse growth, is it actually worth building — i.e. does it amortize
against the cost of generating its training data — and what are its limits?

report.title: sm-02-utility-and-limits — amortized value of the cheap emulator
report.evidence_quality: measured emulator + simulator timings; amortized break-even; learnability limit from sm-01
report.objective:
Quantify the practical value of the emulator that sm-01 found actually works
(linear), and state its limits honestly, so "fast" is meaningful rather than
an apples-to-oranges speedup.
report.setup:
code/utility_demo.py fits the linear emulator on the compact dataset, sweeps
5,000 initial conditions × 250 steps (timed), and computes the amortized
cost: (8 training sims) + N·(emulator rollout) vs N·(WCM rollout), giving the
break-even N. Simulator per-step time is the measured baseline rate.
report.result:
- Linear emulator: 5,000 × 250-step trajectories in 0.02 s (~0.005 ms/traj).
- Full WCM: ~17 s per 250-step trajectory → the same sweep ≈ 24 h.
- Per-trajectory speedup ≈ 3.8e6×; break-even after ~8 evaluations
  (i.e. the emulator pays back its 8 training sims almost immediately).
Limits (from sm-01): the emulator is valid only for the smooth, low-dim
observables; the broad 11.5k-observable panel is unlearnable from the
observable view (0% beat persistence), and emulation says nothing about
events outside the training distribution (e.g. division — a documented
follow-up).
report.interpretation:
The expensive part of surrogate modeling is generating training data, not the
emulator. Once you've paid for a handful of baseline simulations, a cheap
emulator of a smooth observable is worth building even when a neural net adds
nothing — it turns a 24-hour sweep into 0.02 s. The discipline is to scope it
to what's actually emulable and to amortize honestly.
report.decision:
PASS — the cheap emulator amortizes after ~8 evaluations and its limits are
stated explicitly.

conclusion_verdicts.claim: A cheap emulator of a smooth observable is worth building once training data exists.
Emulation extends to the cell's high-dimensional hidden state.
conclusion_verdicts.basis: sm-01: 0% of broad observables beat persistence; not learnable from the view.

falsifiability:
The utility claim fails if the emulator does not amortize within a small number
of evaluations, or if its per-trajectory cost is not far below the WCM's.
